New data projects an electoral funding windfall for One Nation over the next five years, as scrutiny increases on the party’s financial management.

Pauline Hanson’s One Nation stands to receive $219 million in taxpayer funding over the next five years, according to modelling based on current polling and changes to funding laws.

The projected windfall comes as Adelaide Magistrates Court forces One Nation to repay a former candidate thousands of dollars in campaign spending. In a separate case, Hanson could be held personally liable for failing to lodge party financial statements over the past three years.

“You could fill a town hall with the people she has short-changed,” says former One Nation South Australia leader Jennifer Game, who won a $15,000 settlement on Thursday.

“I think people should know that there are two sides, ultimately, to Pauline. There’s a lot of positive qualities about her, you know, that I could talk about; but equally, the way in which candidates and others are dealt with is pretty grim.”

Game tells The Saturday Paper she was forced to sign a candidate contract that placed a range of restrictions on her and required her to source campaign materials centrally.

“In my case, for example, my contract said that for the 2025 election, I had to take 1500 corflutes,” Game says. “Well, they’re banned in South Australia. You can’t put them up, you can only use them at polling booths in the week of the election. So I said, ‘Look, I don’t need these, I don’t want them.’ But I had to buy them, otherwise they wouldn’t let me stand as a candidate. So I had 1500 corflutes just sitting in my garage that I then had to pay [for them] to be taken to the tip.”

Game is especially critical of a centralised party structure that essentially gives Hanson and her chief of staff, James Ashby, control of the entire party apparatus. It is to this structure that the projected $219 million in campaign funding will be paid over the next five years.

“Everything’s done centrally. It’s all highly controlled; it’s not an organisation you can scale up, like a normal party,” Game says. “You could go to the Labor Party now, and they’ve got the processes, they’ve got the checks and balances in place to handle money and policy committees … They all have people who have accounting and legal backgrounds, but none of these checks and balances exist in One Nation.

“There’s Alex Jones, who’s their treasurer. I mean, he was in his early 20s when he first came on board, he has no qualifications regarding the handling of money, and I say that as someone who has a tax law degree and practised for a long time. And then there’s Pauline and James, and until recently, of course, there was Sean Black, the convicted rapist.”

Jones pleaded guilty in 2022 to one count of attempting to defraud the Queensland Electoral Commission over campaign funding, although a conviction was not recorded. Black was jailed in 2018 for rape and assault.

“It’s a party legally, I guess,” Game says. “But it’s not a party in the traditional sense of the word, which is why it all fell apart back in 1998 or whatever, and it will fall apart this time, because at the end of the day, Pauline trusts no one and cannot delegate power to anyone outside that very tight inner circle.”

Ashby, Hanson’s long-time chief of staff, dismisses concerns over One Nation’s centralised structure, and rejected claims candidates had to choose a nominated supplier for campaign material.

“The reason we’ve steered candidates to use businesses vetted by the party is that we guarantee quality and price,” Ashby tells The Saturday Paper.

“Candidates are welcome to use other suppliers, but often they can’t match wholesale rates we’ve negotiated with larger suppliers.”

Ashby’s comments follow a secret 2017 recording, made at a meeting also attended by Hanson, where he raised the idea of doubling the price of candidate advertising packages on invoices to be claimed back from the Queensland Electoral Commission.

“There is an opportunity for us to make some money on this if we play this smart,” Ashby was recorded saying. “I will deny I ever said this, but what stops us from getting a middleman or gracing … I am happy to grace in cash, double the price of whatever it is.”

Ashby later said the comments were part of “a brainstorming session that has been taken right out of context”.

The latest, huge spike in projected funding for One Nation is made possible by the introduction of state and federal laws that increase public funding for political parties to reduce their reliance on private donations.

“You could go to the Labor Party now, and they’ve got the processes, they’ve got the checks and balances in place to handle money and policy committees … but none of these checks and balances exist in One Nation.”

The Electoral Legislation Amendment (Electoral Reform) Act 2025, due to take effect on January 1, 2027, will raise the per-vote public funding rate to $5 for every first-preference vote, a 48 per cent increase on the $3.386 rate that applied at the 2025 election.

“A system, purportedly designed to increase trust in elections, has become a mechanism to exclude newcomers and protect the political establishment – of which One Nation is a member – from competition even as the major party vote is in permanent decline,” says Climate 200 convenor Simon Holmes à Court, who produced the modelling.

“It’s as if the winner of the grand final got to make the rules for the next season and gave first draft picks and the gate takings to just the final four. Everyone would lose interest in the game quickly – but politics is too important to us all to be a game, let alone a rigged game.”

The modelling is based on an aggregate across federal and state elections starting from this year’s South Australian election through to the expected 2031 federal election.

At the May 2025 federal election, One Nation received 991,814 first-preference votes, or 6.4 per cent of the total, in the House of Representatives, and 899,296, or 5.7 per cent of the total, in the Senate. Under the funding rules then in force, the party received $3.386 for every eligible first-preference vote for candidates who cleared the 4 per cent hurdle, yielding just over $6 million in public funding.

At the South Australian election on March 21, One Nation achieved a primary vote of 22.9 per cent, winning three Legislative Council seats and four House of Assembly seats. Under South Australia’s generous public funding laws, on which the new federal laws are largely based, One Nation banked $7.3 million.

Six weeks later, One Nation’s David Farley swept to victory in the Farrer byelection triggered by the resignation of former Liberal leader Sussan Ley, ending the Coalition’s 77-year hold on the seat.

In funding terms it was a modest result. The byelection saw One Nation receive $140,107 in public funding, paid at the current rate of $3.499 per vote, but its political significance was enormous, with One Nation winning its first federal lower house seat in 30 years.

“One Nation has reached the end of its beginning,” Farley told supporters in Albury that night. “We’re going through the ceiling from here.”

Labor’s electoral funding legislation, which passed with Coalition support last February, also introduces a new system of administrative assistance funding – $30,000 a year for each member of the House of Representatives, and $15,000 a year for each senator. It is paid in advance, with no cap on the number of parliamentary members a party holds.

With One Nation’s representation in Canberra already numbering six, that means from January 1 through to the next election, due in May 2028, One Nation will receive $183,000 in administrative funding alone.

Victoria, where voters will head to the polls in November and which has its own generous public funding arrangements, will represent the biggest opportunity so far for One Nation to increase its cut of electoral funding.

Based on the Freshwater poll from June 2026, the Climate 200 modelling estimates One Nation’s Victorian public funding entitlement at $38.5 million, which would represent the biggest state-level figure in the entire five-year window.

In New South Wales, where Labor Premier Chris Minns will ask voters to give his government a second term in March next year, Climate 200’s modelling uses the May Resolve poll data to project a funding entitlement of $33.8 million.

Together, Victoria and NSW account for more than $72 million of the $219 million total.

It is the 2028 federal election that has the potential to deliver One Nation the biggest windfall, however.

With the latest Newspoll, conducted from June 1-4, putting One Nation’s primary vote at 31 per cent, Climate 200’s model scales up the 2025 results and distributes the swing across all 150 lower house seats and the eight state and territory Senate contests, using the same preferential and proportional counts as the Australian Electoral Commission.

On that basis, the model projects One Nation winning 58 seats in the House of Representatives and 12 of the 40 Senate seats turning over at the next election, giving it a total of 15 senators.

Applied to its projected 2028 vote tally, the new $5 a vote rate would see One Nation entitled to about $50.7 million, about eight times One Nation’s 2025 public funding.

With a post-2028 election party room comprising 73 MPs and senators, One Nation would receive a further $6.3 million in administrative funding on top of its per-vote entitlement.

Queensland goes to the polls in October 2028, with the Climate 200 modelling projecting a funding entitlement of $14.2 million. Western Australia follows in March 2029, with public funding projected at $5.1 million. South Australia returns to the polls in March 2030, with public funding projected at $6.1 million.

In Victoria, where another state election will be due in November 2030, Climate 200 projects public funding worth $17.6 million. NSW taxpayers could kick in an extra $11.6 million at the March 2031 state election.

Looking ahead to the 2031 federal election, which, if this parliament and the next parliament both run the full three years would be due in May 2031, Holmes à Court’s modelling projects that if One Nation’s primary vote held at the current level of 31 per cent, it would generate a per-vote public funding entitlement of $57,294,880, calculated at the indexed $5 a vote base rate.

The huge increase in public funding is likely to present something of a dilemma for Hanson, who has previously signalled her strong opposition to political parties accepting public funding.

“If you are really serious about it, stop putting your hand out and taking the electoral funding every time an election’s held, because the people are fed up with it,” Hanson told the Senate in 2018.

“It’s take, take, take. That’s what people see from this house all the time, that you’re not prepared to be up-front and honest with the Australian people.”

Special Minister of State Don Farrell, the architect of the new federal funding laws, says the headline figure that could potentially flow through to One Nation disguises the onerous transparency obligations and other strict requirements that the new laws place on political parties.

“Under Labor’s reforms, everything is transparent and visible. The public will see who is funding election campaigns and where that money is spent,” Farrell tells The Saturday Paper.

“Under changes fought and won by Labor, you cannot claim public funding unless you can show that money has been spent appropriately – no politician or party should profit off taxpayer funds.”

Senator Farrell argues that the new laws make it much harder for wealthy individuals to exert oversized influence on political parties and their elected representatives. “This is a clear choice. We can have a robust system of public funding, or we can have campaigns flooded with donations from billionaires playing politics.”

Beyond the increased per-vote rate and new administrative funding, the Electoral Reform Act also introduces major changes to donations.

From January 1 donations above $5000 must be disclosed, with expedited reporting requirements kicking in during election periods, and as quickly as within 24 hours in the final days of a campaign.

Private donations are capped at $50,000 per person per recipient per year, with an overall cap of $1.6 million across all recipients.

Electoral expenditure is also capped, with a $90 million ceiling on total spending by a registered political party and its associated entities and an $800,000 limit per division.

“Australia has one of the best voting systems in the world – compulsory preferential voting, no gerrymandering and a trusted ballot – but our democracy is far from perfect,” says Holmes à Court.

“Over the last 15 years, the legacy parties have built a massive wall of advantage around themselves, almost impossible for outsiders to climb, and with the threat of newcomers, the legacy parties use public money to raise the wall and build moats … The upshot is less choice for voters, and a ballot paper where the only viable candidates are those chosen by those already in power.”

Jason Koutsoukis is The Saturday Paper’s special correspondent.
